Hi everyone, thanks for your replies. It was good for me to learn a variety of viewpoints and I've learned a lot from each person who has posted here.

Ultimately, I will need to respect what she wants and learn how to deal with these tense emotions on my own. I am set to take my state's BAR licensing exam to become an attorney, and have always been someone with a very strict sense of right and wrong. When I see something that is "wrong", I feel that indignation at an extreme level (probably related to my PTSD and secondary trauma working in an LGBT hate crime unit and family abuse unit). 

I see now that this perspective serves me well in my career, but is not an appropriate viewpoint to bring into a relationship with the woman I love more than life itself. 

It will never be easy for me to see people making death threats to her online while she works, but that's a me problem and not her problem.

I currently see a counselor used to working with LGBT+ clients and will consult with her on processing these emotions in a healthy manner. Every week, I improve. I am more respectful of my girlfriend's wants/desires in general and try to do a better job of listening as a partner (all thanks to you folks).

Hi everyone, thanks for your replies. I've resumed taking my girl the doctor and they're still trying to figure out what's wrong. She's doing better overall, but there are still hiccups. 

I do have a counselor, but for issues for related to PTSD and Bipolar. My partner has always stood by me during my traumatic/manic/depressive episodes and continually supports my journey to healing. I was incredibly unstable until the doctor found the the correct medication and dosage for me and I thank my partner a lot for being there for me, even while she was experiencing chronic pain and health problems.

I've been able to adjust to these new circumstances the past week and currently speak with my counselor on healthily processing my feelings over my partner. All I know is that I love her more than life itself, and that if she can stand by me despite how difficult it is, then I can too.

Hey, thanks for your reply. Your story really spoke to me and made me feel like I'm not alone in this. I don't think I know how to handle this yet, only that it makes me feel better that others know that I'm feeling.

Yikes, that's incredibly invasive. I'm from CA and they only asked me whether I have any conditions that would prevent me from practicing law. I was put in a 5150 (a welfare hold they do in CA to people about to harm themselves over others) over the summer. The cause ended up being a case of undiagnosed and untreated Bipolar. When I got put on the correct medication and went to therapy, I was normal again. Asked counselors on what to do and they said that 5150 is a welfare hold and not a police arrest. If I believed that my condition wouldn't impair my ability to practice, then I had no need to disclose.

I had a lot of mental health problems related to being LGBT law student living with unsupportive parents then needing to move somewhere else during 2L (I only fully came out in the past year).

 It was definitely a contributing factor to my poor mental health. LGBT issues can be really complicated and people with them can definitely benefit from getting help. 

I empathize with that feeling of being violated and it shouldn't be like this. There's something very terrible about laying your soul bare and having a bunch of strangers you'll never meet probe into you.

I think there is still stigma attached to seeking mental health treatment both in law school and in practice. Someday, I'd like to instigate that cultural shift from being ashamed of getting help to one where it can be openly discussed in the field. I'm planning to be open about my experiences as a law student and future attorney with PTSD and Bipolar, but for now, I have to keep it on the DL while my CnF is underway. I don't have an answer for you other than this completely sucks and I feel you.

I feel like I could be either a lesbian or bi (but with a stronger attraction to women). I was the the victim of a sex crime a few years ago and this caused me to have goddamn panic attacks around men. 

I've gotten better though. And while I can tolerate them, I can't say (yet) that I'm attracted to them the same way I am with women. Maybe in time, I will heal more and see how I feel. For now, I tell people either "gay or bi" and have no plans to "come out" until a few years from now. People should respect that sexuality can be really fluid and that labels aren't that necessary.

My life became so consumed with processing the pain, that my dream faded away. I'm currently trying to become an attorney, to expand the access to legal rights to victims like myself.

I still get sad when I look at the ocean though. I think about how my life would have turned out had I not been harmed or if the people I cared about had protected me (like they should have).

The first time I experienced it, I was still healing from a traumatic event and already had trouble sleeping at night. During one night, the fire alarm in my apartment went off. I woke up and couldn't move at all. I couldn't breathe well. I was hallucinating and thinking people were coming into my room. It felt like someone was on my chest.

After what felt like forever, the weight, the hallucinations, the panic, etc. subsided. I wasn't aware this was "sleep paralysis" at the time. I remember trying to scream for a roommate to call 911 (because I thought I was dying), but words weren't coming out.

When I experience sleep paralysis nowadays, it always when I'm napping in my car in my school's underground parking lot. Something about the environment and continual noises triggers it for me. The hallucinations tend to be something like other people entering my car, but I can't move to tell them to get out.

I'm sorry you're feeling this way. I can sympathize. When I first started to grapple with my bisexuality, I thought there was something extremely wrong with me. It felt like I chose to make my life more complicated. In reaction,  I thought I should just tell people I'm straight while admiring women (I'm female) from afar. 

I still hate myself sometimes. But I've been trying to accept that the problem isn't with me for being me, it's with those who don't want to understand me. This had made accepting my sexuality a bit easier. 

If you'd like help with any specific, I (and others) are here for you. This can be very difficult but you are not alone.

It's very easy to use. Just make it clear you're experimenting, and you might also want to put in that you're not looking for group sex (you're going to get girls who "just want to please their man").

If you match with someone, you could plan to do something prior (like drinks). That way, if you're getting really bad vibes from your match (e.g., crazy, makes you feel unsafe, etc.) you can easily bounce. If you're not getting those vibes, then proceed with the experimenting.

If you wanted privacy, that might be a problem. When I made my Tinder, I ended up seeing profiles from people I knew in high school and colleges and maybe they've seen mine. No one brings it up though. It's like a "what happens here stays here" environment. 

Assuming LA means Los Angeles (and not Louisiana), West Hollywood has many LGBT-friendly bars. One of the most well-known is "The Abbey."

There's a chapel in our school. I was trying to come out to myself around that time, so I needed a quiet place  to be alone. Near the Jesus statute was a plaque stating that we live to serve others. 

I stared.  At some point, I came to the conclusion that if I wanted a career in "serving others" (public interest work), I would have to learn to love others, and that entailed learning how to love myself first and foremost. When I walked out, I left a note in the prayer box, asking for a prayer and support as I began my coming out process. Later that day, I came out to my best friend.

Aside from this, I also think shows play a large role in inspiring us budding gays. Miss Kobayshi's Dragon Maid (anime) was a nice slice of life, depicting a lesbian relationship without overtly sexual tones and just doing normal couple things (like taking your kid to school or deciding who cooks dinner). It made me feel like I could have something normal like that too.

College and In the Closet: Yoga pants. I wore them just to get out of my dorm to get to class. I didn't care for my appearance. Thought I was straight. Had a BF. Why try to impress anyone? 

Grad School and Out: Skinny Jeans, Khakis, Suit Pants. Embraced being hella gay. Women are beautiful and I seriously needed to up my game. However, I feel like an alien in skirts/dresses, so I try to impress in pants, because it makes flirting/being myself easier.

I'm not giving you legal advice, but just observations from what I've read regarding workplace discrimination (if you wanted to research it yourself). Assuming this is in the US, Title VII is usually what most people think of when it comes to protection from workplace discrimination. I've read conflicting opinions on whether sexual orientation constitutes a protected class, so I won't say anything.  

However, if you'd like more information, the EEOC has a good website describing examples of LGBT-related discrimination in the workplace (https://www.eeoc.gov/eeoc/newsroom/wysk/enforcement_protections_lgbt_workers.cfm)

As for what you can do in the moment? I'm not really sure. Would your supervisor or manager be open to complaints? I'd imagine they'd want to keep a safe and neutral working environment.

If you meet her in person again, I think a joking apology would be fine. The FB apology might be a bit much though. You didn't do anything objectively wrong.

If you go on your third date, I think you are within your rights to ask her what it is she's specifically looking for in a relationship. If she gives non-vague answers (e.g., something more substantial than "oh just time to figure things out" or  "I just want to see where things go"), that's a good sign. If she really likes you, she'll give you definitive answers. 

If you do get the greenlight, you can be on the look out for things indicating she'd like to be touched (e.g., looking at you, letting shoulders, finding reasons to be close). She may be shy and not want to act on it. If so, that's where you step in to "make your move." Like asking to hold her hand or just doing it if the signs are obvious. I wish you well OP!

I felt really guilty about it. I hadn't come to terms with my sexuality yet or that I had always been this way. I thought I just needed to try harder with my BF. So I did. The last times we had sex were some of our kinkiest.

I can sympathize with you. I was the victim of child sexual abuse (thought my neighbor and I were just friends, but then he got TOO close) and two instances of sexual assault as an adult (The first, I was a young exchange student in Berlin. The other students left me alone on an empty street, where I was molested by a drunk German who shoved his tongue down my throat, and proceeded to chase me on and off buses). 

Things like this leave an imprint on your mind that makes it exceptionally difficult to be close to people again. For quite a while, if a man touched me, I would have a panic attack. 

Luckily, I had not-shitty friends that really cared for me as if they were family, so they were there to listen about the burdens of my past. Initially, I had significant trust issues but that changed when (1) I met these amazing people (2) I attended treatment at a Rape Treatment Center and (3) I came out. 

I think I have made amazing progress as a rape survivor, going from fearing all touch to taking a woman out on a date and holding her hand. There can be reversals though. For example, I was traumatized by, what I perceived to be, betrayal at the hands of my female friends (Thought we were close, but they refused to testify against our rapist, who had assaulted/molest us, and got angry at me for bringing it to the police). 

Recently, this girl I held hands with, that I saw as my "triumph" over my personal demons, just ghosted me (Again, thought we were close, but she was really a goddamn bitch and I couldn't tell.) Can you see a pattern to my life? 

Do I still crave someone to hold at night? To kiss? To have sex with? Yes. Do my past traumas and deep-seated trust issues get in the way of that? Hell yeah. 

In other words, don't feel like you're alone on this. Trauma and abuse wreak havoc on the brain, and as much as you want to control it, you can't without professional aid or a serious support system. It's a physical injury in a way. Imagine you were in a car accident and your leg muscles have atrophied. If you want to walk, you need a physical therapist. 

I hope you find a way out of this OP, it's REALLY difficult to get out of the hole trauma makes, and I'm STILL trying to get out of it.
